content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
107	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
108	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
109	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
110	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
111	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
112	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
113	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
114	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
115	the usual `409 conflict`.
116	
117	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
118	hold:
119	
120	```http
121	PUT /quotas
122	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
123	X-Tenant-Id: acme
124	
125	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
126	```
127	
128	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
129	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
130	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
131	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
132	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
133	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
134	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
135	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
136	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
137	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
138	
139	```http
140	GET /quotas
141	X-Tenant-Id: acme
142	```
143	
144	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
145	when the tenant has declared none.
146	
147	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
148	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
149	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
150	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
151	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
152	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
153	
154	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
155	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
156	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
157	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
158	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
159	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
160	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
161	
162	### Usage metering and billing
163	
164	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
165	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
166	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
167	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
168	metered action types are:
169	
170	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
171	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
172	  definition;
173	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
174	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
175	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
176	  `schedule_triggered`;
177	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
178	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
179	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
180	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
181	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
182	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
183	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
184	  meters nothing.
185	
186	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
187	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
188	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
189	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
190	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
191	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
192	
193	```http
194	GET /usage
195	X-Tenant-Id: acme
196	```
197	
198	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
199	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
200	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
201	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
202	
203	```http
204	GET /bill
205	X-Tenant-Id: acme
206	```
207	
208	Returns the per-type bill:
209	
210	```json
211	{"bill":{"items":[
212	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
213	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
214	],"total":2100}}
215	```
216	
217	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
218	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
219	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
220	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
221	
222	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
223	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
224	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
225	
226	### Operational metrics
227	
228	```http
229	GET /metrics
230	X-Tenant-Id: acme
231	```
232	
233	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
234	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
235	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
236	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
237	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
238	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
239	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
240	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
241	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
242	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
243	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
244	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
245	
246	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
247	timestamp ending in `Z`:
248	
249	```http
250	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
251	X-Tenant-Id: acme
252	```
253	
254	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
255	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
256	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
257	  counts every recorded fact;
258	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
259	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
260	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
261	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
262	  result.
263	
264	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
265	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
266	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
267	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
268	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
269	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
270	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
271	completion or termination event.
272	
273	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
274	
275	```http
276	GET /metrics/export
277	X-Tenant-Id: acme
278	```
279	
280	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
281	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
282	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
283	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
284	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
285	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
286	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
287	
288	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
289	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
290	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
291	ordered by ascending label value:
292	
293	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
294	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
295	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
296	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
297	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
298	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
299	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
300	  unlabeled scalar samples.
301	
302	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
303	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
304	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
305	ends with a single newline.
306	
307	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
308	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
309	failures, and schedule triggers:
310	
311	```json
312	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
313	```
314	
315	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
316	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
317	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
318	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
319	  ended for that reason.
320	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
321	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
322	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
323	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
324	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
325	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
326	  another attempt, per node identifier.
327	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
328	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
329	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
330	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
331	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
332	
333	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
334	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
335	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
336	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
337	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
338	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
339	
340	### Health
341	
342	```http
343	GET /health
344	```
345	
346	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
347	
348	### Create a workflow
349	
350	```http
351	POST /workflows
352	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
353	
354	{
355	  "id": "order-flow",
356	  "nodes": [
357	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
358	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
359	  ]
360	}
361	```
362	
363	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
364	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
365	
366	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
367	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
368	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
369	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
370	
371	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
372	
373	```json
374	{
375	  "id": "order-flow",
376	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
377	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
378	}
379	```
380	
381	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
382	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
383	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
384	
385	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
386	
387	```json
388	{
389	  "id": "nightly-orders",
390	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
391	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
392	}
393	```
394	
395	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
396	
397	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
398	
399	```json
400	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
401	```
402	
403	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
404	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
405	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
406	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
407	`false`.
408	
409	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
410	
411	```json
412	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
413	```
414	
415	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
416	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
417	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
418	dependencies of its successors.
419	
420	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
421	
422	```json
423	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
424	```
425	
426	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
427	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
428	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
429	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
430	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
431	`retries_exhausted`.
432	
433	A task may instead declare an approval point:
434	
435	```json
436	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
437	```
438	
439	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
440	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
441	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
442	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
443	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
444	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
445	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
446	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
447	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
448	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
449	move the task.
450	
451	### Submit an approval decision
452	
453	```http
454	POST /executions/run-1/decision
455	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
456	
457	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
458	```
459	
460	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
461	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
462	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
463	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
464	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
465	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
466	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
467	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
468	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
469	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
470	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
471	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
472	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
473	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
474	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
475	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
476	404.
477	
478	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
479	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
480	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
481	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
482	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
483	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
484	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
485	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
486	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
487	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
488	shape and event stream.
489	
490	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
491	segment:
492	
493	```json
494	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
495	```
496	
497	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
498	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
499	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
500	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
501	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
502	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
503	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
504	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
505	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
506	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
507	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
508	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
509	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
510	loop node instead).
511	
512	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
513	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
514	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
515	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
516	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
517	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
518	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
519	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
520	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
521	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
522	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
523	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
524	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
525	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
526	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
527	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
528	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
529	belong only to their iterations.
530	
531	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
532	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
533	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
534	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
535	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
536	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
537	exactly.
538	
539	### Dynamic map nodes
540	
541	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
542	recorded array:
543	
544	```json
545	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
546	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
547	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
548	```
549	
550	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
551	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
552	
553	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
554	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
555	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
556	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
557	  the same path syntax as a condition.
558	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
559	  expand.
560	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
561	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
562	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
563	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
564	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
565	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
566	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
567	
568	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
569	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
570	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
571	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
572	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
573	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
574	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
575	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
576	overwrite another instance.
577	
578	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
579	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
580	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
581	become available in the usual way.
582	
583	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
584	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
585	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
586	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
587	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
588	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
589	
590	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
591	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
592	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
593	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
594	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
595	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
596	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
597	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
598	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
599	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
600	
601	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
602	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
603	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
604	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
605	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
606	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
607	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
608	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
609	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
610	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
611	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
612	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
613	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
614	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
615	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
616	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
617	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
618	
619	### Maps inside loop bodies
620	
621	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
622	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
623	other body member:
624	
625	```json
626	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
627	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
628	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
629	```
630	
631	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
632	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
633	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
634	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
635	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
636	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
637	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
638	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
639	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
640	
641	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
642	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
643	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
644	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
645	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
646	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
647	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
648	influence from the iteration number.
649	
650	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
651	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
652	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
653	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
654	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
655	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
656	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
657	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
658	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
659	
660	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
661	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
662	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
663	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
664	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
665	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
666	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
667	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
668	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
669	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
670	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
671	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
672	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
673	
674	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
675	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
676	
677	### Delete and modify expanded instances
678	
679	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
680	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
681	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
682	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
683	
684	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
685	that has permanently failed:
686	
687	```http
688	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
689	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
690	
691	{}
692	```
693	
694	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
695	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
696	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
697	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
698	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
699	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
700	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
701	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
702	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
703	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
704	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
705	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
706	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
707	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
708	
709	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
710	before it is worked:
711	
712	```http
713	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
714	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
715	
716	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
717	```
718	
719	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
720	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
721	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
722	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
723	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
724	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
725	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
726	is stored verbatim.
727	
728	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
729	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
730	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
731	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
732	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
733	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
734	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
735	
736	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
737	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
738	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
739	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
740	carries no loop context.
741	
742	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
743	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
744	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
745	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
746	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
747	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
748	first result and appends no second event.
749	
750	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
751	
752	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
753	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
754	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
755	  and `iteration`;
756	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
757	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
758	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
759	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
760	
761	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
762	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
763	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
764	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
765	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
766	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
767	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
768	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
769	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
770	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
771	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
772	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
773	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
774	
775	### Re-expand a dynamic node
776	
777	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
778	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
779	
780	```http
781	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
782	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
783	
784	{}
785	```
786	
787	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
788	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
789	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
790	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
791	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
792	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
793	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
794	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
795	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
796	bounds start from zero.
797	
798	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
799	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
800	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
801	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
802	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
803	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
804	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
805	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
806	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
807	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
808	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
809	expansion.
810	
811	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
812	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
813	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
814	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
815	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
816	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
817	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
818	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
819	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
820	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
821	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
822	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
823	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
824	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
825	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
826	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
827	an instance that stayed deleted.
828	
829	### Workflow versions
830	
831	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
832	
833	```json
834	{
835	  "id": "order-flow",
836	  "version": "2026-09-25",
837	  "nodes": [
838	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
839	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
840	  ]
841	}
842	```
843	
844	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
845	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
846	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
847	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
848	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
849	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
850	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
851	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
852	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
853	
854	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
855	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
856	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
857	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
858	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
859	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
860	
861	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
862	current version at the moment it starts:
863	
864	```http
865	POST /executions
866	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
867	
868	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
869	```
870	
871	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
872	
873	```json
874	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
875	```
876	
877	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
878	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
879	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
880	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
881	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
882	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
883	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
884	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
885	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
886	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
887	conclusions never change.
888	
889	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
890	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
891	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
892	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
893	stream with no added field.
894	
895	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
896	
897	```http
898	GET /workflows/order-flow
899	```
900	
901	```json
902	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
903	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
904	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
905	]}
906	```
907	
908	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
909	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
910	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
911	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
912	resources as usual.

914	### Migrate a running execution to another version
915	
916	```http
917	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
918	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
919	
920	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
921	```
922	
923	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
924	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
925	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
926	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
927	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
928	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
929	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
930	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
931	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
932	carries the target version.
933	
934	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
935	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
936	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
937	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
938	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
939	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
940	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
941	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
942	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
943	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
944	
945	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
946	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
947	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
948	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
949	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
950	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
951	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
952	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
953	content.
954	
955	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
956	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
957	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
958	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
959	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
960	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
961	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
962	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
963	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
964	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
965	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
966	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
967	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
968	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.

1001	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",

1007	### List workflows
1008	
1009	```http
1010	GET /workflows?limit=50
1011	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1012	```
1013	
1014	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1015	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1016	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1017	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1018	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1019	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1020	state.
1021	
1022	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1023	
1024	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1025	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1026	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1027	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1028	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1029	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1030	  returns the definite empty list.

1032	### List executions
1033	
1034	```http
1035	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1036	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1037	```
1038	
1039	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1040	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1041	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1042	or `terminated`, always a string), and its `termination_reason` (one of the
1043	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`). A
1044	namespace with no executions gets the definite empty result
1045	`{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is read-only and
1046	never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a checkpoint, or
1047	records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and change no state
1048	or metering conclusion.
1049	
1050	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1051	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, three
1052	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1053	
1054	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1055	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1056	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1057	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1058	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1059	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1060	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1061	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1062	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1063	  `400 validation_error`.
1064	
1065	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1066	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1067	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1068	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1069	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1070	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.

1072	### Inspect an execution
1073	
1074	```http
1075	GET /executions/run-1
1076	GET /executions/run-1/events
1077	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1078	```
1079	
1080	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1081	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1082	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1083	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1084	
1085	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1086	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1087	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1088	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1089	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1090	
1091	```http
1092	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1093	```
1094	
1095	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1096	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1097	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1098	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1099	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1100	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1101	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1102	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1103	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1104	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1105	  order.
1106	
1107	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1108	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1109	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1110	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1111	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1112	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1113	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1114	`404 not_found`.

1116	### Webhook notifications
1117	
1118	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1119	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1120	
1121	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1122	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1123	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1124	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1125	  reason);
1126	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1127	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1128	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1129	
1130	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1131	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1132	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1133	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1134	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1135	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1136	subscriptions" below.
1137	
1138	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1139	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1140	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1141	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1142	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1143	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1144	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1145	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1146	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1147	triggered it.
1148	
1149	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1150	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1151	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1152	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1153	results as before.
1154	
1155	### Inspect the delivery history
1156	
1157	```http
1158	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1159	```
1160	
1161	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1162	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1163	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1164	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1165	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1166	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1167	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1168	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1169	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1170	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1171	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1172	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1173	
1174	### Queue subscriptions
1175	
1176	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1177	
1178	```json
1179	{
1180	  "id": "run-4",
1181	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1182	  "input": {},
1183	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1184	}
1185	```
1186	
1187	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1188	
1189	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1190	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1191	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1192	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1193	
1194	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1195	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1196	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1197	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1198	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1199	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1200	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1201	
1202	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1203	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1204	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1205	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1206	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1207	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1208	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1209	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1210	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1211	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1212	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1213	before.
1214	
1215	### Inspect the queue state
1216	
1217	```http
1218	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1219	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1220	```
1221	
1222	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1223	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1224	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1225	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1226	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1227	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1228	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1229	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1230	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1231	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1232	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1233	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1234	
1235	### Pull messages from a queue
1236	
1237	```http
1238	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1239	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1240	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1241	
1242	{}
1243	```
1244	
1245	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1246	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1247	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1248	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1249	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1250	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1251	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1252	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1253	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1254	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1255	
1256	### Acknowledge a message
1257	
1258	```http
1259	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1260	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
1261	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1262	
1263	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
1264	```
1265	
1266	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
1267	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
1268	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
1269	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
1270	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
1271	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
1272	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
1273	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
1274	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
1275	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
1276	`conflict`.

1278	### Schedules
1279	
1280	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
1281	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
1282	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
1283	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
1284	
1285	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
1286	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
1287	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
1288	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
1289	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
1290	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
1291	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
1292	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
1293	
1294	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
1295	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
1296	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
1297	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
1298	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
1299	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
1300	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
1301	created is exposed through the status query below.
1302	
1303	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
1304	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
1305	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
1306	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
1307	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
1308	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
1309	
1310	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
1311	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
1312	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
1313	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
1314	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
1315	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1316	
1317	### Declare or replace a schedule
1318	
1319	```http
1320	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1321	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
1322	
1323	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
1324	```
1325	
1326	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
1327	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
1328	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
1329	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
1330	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
1331	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
1332	
1333	### Inspect the schedule status
1334	
1335	```http
1336	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1337	```
1338	
1339	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
1340	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
1341	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
1342	
1343	```json
1344	{
1345	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1346	  "paused": false,
1347	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
1348	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
1349	}
1350	```
1351	
1352	The fields are:
1353	
1354	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
1355	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
1356	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
1357	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
1358	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
1359	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
1360	  `null` until the first period fires;
1361	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
1362	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
1363	
1364	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
1365	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.

1367	### Preview upcoming triggers
1368	
1369	```http
1370	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/preview?limit=3
1371	```
1372	
1373	Returns the trigger times the declared plan would settle next, starting
1374	from the first period that has not been settled yet, together with the
1375	input each created execution would carry:
1376	
1377	```json
1378	{
1379	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1380	  "previews": [
1381	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T09:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}},
1382	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T10:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}},
1383	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T11:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}}
1384	  ]
1385	}
1386	```
1387	
1388	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored, like the status query;
1389	- `previews`: up to `limit` entries in ascending time order, each carrying
1390	  `trigger_at` (an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`) and `input`
1391	  (the declared input object verbatim).
1392	
1393	A fixed interval projects continuously from the next unsettled period; a
1394	cron plan takes the next minute matching its field rules, then the one
1395	after that, and so on. The `limit` query parameter is required, must be a
1396	positive integer, and may appear at most once; a missing, repeated, or
1397	malformed value — or any other query parameter — is a 400
1398	`validation_error`. The preview is read-only: it creates no execution,
1399	appends no event, and never moves the schedule's cursor, so repeating the
1400	query returns the same projection. A paused schedule projects exactly like
1401	a running one — the missed policy only governs whether a due period
1402	creates an execution, never the projection. A workflow that never declared
1403	a schedule returns the definite empty result `{"schedule":null}`, exactly
1404	like the status query; a missing or cross-tenant workflow returns 404
1405	`not_found`.

1413	{}
1414	```

1420	{}

1423	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
1424	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
1425	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
1426	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
1427	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
1428	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
1429	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1430	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1431	
1432	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1433	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1434	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
1435	
1436	### Checkpoints
1437	
1438	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
1439	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
1440	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
1441	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
1442	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
1443	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
1444	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
1445	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
1446	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
1447	duplicating any node output.
1448	
1449	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
